subject: Cooking
title: The Bread That Started a Revolution
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Bread That Started a Revolution.

hook.text: 'Let them eat cake' — Marie Antoinette probably never said it. But bread did start the French Revolution.

buildup.text: In 1789, bread consumed 80% of a French worker's wages. A series of bad harvests made it unaffordable.

discovery.text: Women marched from Paris to Versailles demanding bread — forcing King Louis XVI back to the capital.

twist.text: The revolution's first act was fixing bread prices. The new republic guaranteed affordable bread as a right.

climax.text: France still regulates baguette prices today — a legacy of the revolution's bread politics.

punchline.text: The French Revolution wasn't about liberty alone. It was about bread.

quiz.question: What triggered the Women's March to Versailles in 1789?

details.summary: Bread shortages and price spikes directly sparked the French Revolution in 1789. When the price of a four-pound loaf reached 88 percent of a laborer's daily wage, Parisian women marched on Versailles demanding bread.
details.whyItMatters: The French Revolution demonstrates that bread is political. When governments fail to keep bread affordable, revolutions follow. This pattern repeated across history from Rome to the Arab Spring.
takeaways: Bread consumed up to 88 percent of a laborer's wage before the Revolution
Parisian women marched on Versailles demanding bread in October 1789
Marie Antoinette likely never said 'let them eat cake'

faq.question: Did bread prices really cause the French Revolution?
faq.answer: Bread prices were a primary trigger but not the only cause. Failed harvests in 1788 pushed bread prices to crisis levels. Combined with inequality, tax burden, and political frustration, unaffordable bread became the catalyst that transformed simmering resentment into violent revolution.

faq.question: Did Marie Antoinette actually say 'let them eat cake'?
faq.answer: Almost certainly not. The phrase 'qu'ils mangent de la brioche' was attributed to an unnamed princess by Rousseau in 1765, when Marie Antoinette was only nine years old. It was attached to her later as propaganda to vilify the monarchy during the Revolution.
